READING PASSAGE 2 
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 
on pages 6 and 7. 
Catch of the Day 
 Farming marine fish inland will relieve pressure on the oceans 
 
 
A 
In the basement of a building on a wharf in the inner harbor of Baltimore in Maryland, 
USA, a group of aquaculturists at the Institute of Marine and Environmental 
Technology is trying to create an artificial ecosystem. Yonathan Zohar and his 
colleagues hope to liberate the raising of ocean fish from the ocean so that fish can be 
built inland. The fresh, served the day it comes out of the brine (if the brine in question 
is a mixture of tap water and salts), would thus become accessible to millions of people 
who must now have their fish shipped in from afar, deep-frozen. Equally important, 
marine-fish farmers would no longer need to find suitable coastal sites to keep their 
fish while they grow to marketable size, exposing the crowded animals to disease and 
polluting the marine environment. 
 
B 
People have raised freshwater fish in ponds since time immemorial, but farming 
species such as salmon that live mainly in salt water dates back only a few decades, as 
does transformation of saltwater aquaculture to operate on an industrial scale. Now 
fish farming is booming and human consumption of fish has overtaken that of beef. 
Indeed, one way of supplying mankind with enough animal protein in future may be 
through aquaculture. To keep the boom going, technologists like Dr Zohar must 
become more inventive. 
 
C 
Dr Zohar’s ecosystem is about to undergo commercial trials. This ecosystem constantly 
recycles the same supply of brine, which is purified by three sets of bacteria. One set 
turns ammonia excreted by the fish into nitrous ions. A second converts the ions to 
nitrogen and water. A third, working on solid waste filtered from the water, 
transforms it to methane — which via a special generator — provides part of the power 
which keeps the whole thing working. The result is a closed system that can be set up 
anywhere — it generates no pollution and that can be kept disease free. It is also 
escape proof. That means species such as sea bream and sea bass, which cannot be 
grown in North America because they might get out and breed in the wild, could be 
delivered to a table anywhere. Besides transforming the design of fish farms, The 
Institute of Marine and Environmental Technology is also working on extending the 
range of species they can grow. At the institute, Dr Zohar spent decades studying the 
hormone system that triggers spawning* and can now stimulate it on demand. 
 
D 
It is the goal of many fish farmers to supply the fish they are farming with spawnes to 
make them grow more quickly. Indeed, over the past couple of decades researchers

** transgenes: genetic material that has been transferred by genetic engineering techniques 
from one organism to another 
 
have treated more than 35 species of fish in this way. Only one company though, has 
persisted to the point of regulatory approval. AquaBounty’s transgenic Atlantic 
salmon, now cleared both in the USA and Canada, has the desirable property of rapid 
growth. Its transgene**, from the chinook salmon, causes it to put on weight all year 
round not just in spring and summer. That hales the time this fish takes to reach 
marketable size. Finding if people will be willing to eat the result is an experiment is 
own right. However, there is so much natural variation in wild fish that conventional 
selective rearing can make a difference without any hi-tech intervention. In 2007, a 
company which is now part of the Norwegian Institute of Food, Fisheries and 
Aquaculture showed that three decades of this approach by the country’s salmon 
farmers had resulted in fish that grew twice as fast as their wild progenitors. 
 
E 
Researchers at SalmBreed of Bergen, in Norway, have employed genomic selection not 
to create bigger, faster-growing fish but to attack two fish farming’s enemies — 
infestation and infection. Using this technology, have produced varieties of salmon 
resistant to sea lice, pancreas disease and viral illness. 
 
F 
A common complaint by environmental activists is that fish farm does not relieve as 
much pressure on the oceans as it appears, because a lot of the feed it uses is fish meal. 
That simply transfers fishing pressure from species eaten by people directly to those 
that get turned into such meal. But fish meal is expensive, so researchers are trying to 
reduce the amount used by substituting plant matter, such as sova. This initiative has 
seen some success. In 1990, 90% of salmon feed used in Norway was fish meal. In 
2013, the figure was 30%. 
 
G 
Even the production of conventional fish foods results in less strain on the 
environment than food for farm animals. Because fish are cold blooded, they do not eat 
to stay warm. They thus convert more of their food into body mass. For 
conservationists, and those worrying about whether there will be enough food in the 
future to feed the growing human population, that makes fish a particularly attractive 
form of animal protein. 
 
H 
Nevertheless, the demand for all animal protein is growing. Novel technologies are 
therefore being applied to animal husbandry as well. And some imaginative 
researchers are even trying to grow meat and other animal products in factories, 
cutting the animals out of the loop altogether.

Questions 24 – 26 
Complete the summary below. 
Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer. 
Write your answer in boxes 24-26 on your answer sheet. 
Genetic Engineering in Farm Fish 
Genetically engineering fish to grow faster is the 24 ............ of a lot of fish farmers. Now after 
genetic experiments on 35 fish species by various companies, AquaBounty has been granted 
25 ............ to sell its salmon. These fish can increase 26 ............ during each season because 
of the addition of a chinook salmon transgene. However, it has been proven possible to 
greatly increase the rate of fish growth by selective breeding rather than by making use of a 
genetic solution.
